items.title: Creational patterns
items.context: Creational patterns decouple object construction from the system that uses the objects. Singleton ensures a class has exactly one instance. Factory Method lets subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate. Builder constructs a complex object step by step, separating construction from representation.

questions.prompt: Which pattern ensures a class has only one instance, with a global point of access to it?
questions.explanation: Singleton restricts instantiation to exactly one shared instance, typically via a private constructor and a static accessor.

questions.prompt: Which pattern is best suited to constructing a complex object step by step, with many optional parameters?
questions.explanation: Builder separates the construction process from the final representation, letting you assemble a complex object piece by piece (often via chained method calls) instead of one giant constructor.

questions.prompt: Which creational pattern creates new objects by copying an existing instance, rather than instantiating a class directly?
questions.explanation: Prototype clones an existing, fully-configured object to produce a new one — handy when object creation is expensive or complex to reconfigure from scratch.

items.title: Structural patterns
items.context: Structural patterns compose objects into larger structures. Adapter converts one interface into another clients expect. Decorator attaches new behavior to an object dynamically, as an alternative to subclassing. Facade provides a simplified, unified interface to a complex subsystem.

questions.prompt: Which pattern lets an existing class work with a client that expects a different interface, without modifying the original class?
questions.explanation: Adapter wraps the existing class and translates calls into the interface the client actually expects — classic 'square peg into a round hole' bridging.

questions.prompt: Which pattern lets you add responsibilities to an individual object at runtime, without subclassing?
questions.explanation: Decorator wraps an object with another object implementing the same interface, layering extra behavior on top dynamically instead of creating a new subclass for every combination.

questions.prompt: Which pattern's main purpose is to provide a simplified interface to a larger, more complex body of code?
questions.explanation: Facade hides a complex subsystem's many interacting classes behind one simple, unified entry point for clients.

items.title: Behavioral patterns: Observer & Strategy
items.context: Observer defines a one-to-many dependency: when a subject's state changes, all registered observers are notified automatically. Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms and lets the client select which one to use at runtime.

questions.prompt: Which pattern is used when several objects need to be automatically notified whenever a subject's state changes?
questions.explanation: Observer sets up a subscribe/notify relationship — observers register with a subject and are automatically informed whenever it changes state.

questions.prompt: Which pattern lets you swap an algorithm's implementation at runtime, without changing the code that uses it?
questions.explanation: Strategy encapsulates each algorithm behind a common interface, so the client can be handed a different Strategy implementation at runtime without any change to its own code.

items.title: Behavioral patterns: Chain of Responsibility & Command
items.context: Chain of Responsibility passes a request along a chain of handler objects until one handles it (e.g. exception propagation up a call stack). Command encapsulates a request as an object, enabling things like queuing, logging, and undoable operations.

questions.prompt: Which pattern matches this description: multiple objects may handle a request, the handler isn't fixed in advance, and it's acceptable for no one to handle it?
questions.explanation: Chain of Responsibility links potential handlers together; each either handles the request or passes it further down the chain — exactly how exception propagation up the call stack behaves.

questions.prompt: Which pattern encapsulates a request as an object, enabling it to be queued, logged, or undone later?
questions.explanation: Command turns 'do this action' into an object with an execute() method, decoupling the invoker from the receiver — useful for job queues, undo stacks, and callbacks.

items.title: More structural patterns: Proxy & Composite
items.context: Proxy provides a stand-in for another object, controlling access to it (e.g. lazy-loading an expensive object, or checking permissions before delegating). Composite lets clients treat individual objects and compositions of objects (trees) uniformly through a shared interface.

questions.prompt: Which pattern provides a stand-in object that controls access to another object, such as lazily creating it or checking permissions first?
questions.explanation: Proxy implements the same interface as the real object and forwards calls to it, adding a control point — for lazy initialization, access control, remote access, or caching.

questions.prompt: Which pattern lets clients treat a single object and a tree of objects through the same interface?
questions.explanation: Composite defines a common interface for both leaf objects and containers of them, so client code can operate on a whole tree structure without caring whether it's holding one item or a branch of many.

items.title: More behavioral patterns: Template Method & State
items.context: Template Method defines the overall skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, deferring specific steps to subclasses that override them. State lets an object change its behavior when its internal state changes, effectively appearing to change its class at runtime.

questions.prompt: Which pattern defines the fixed skeleton of an algorithm in a base class, letting subclasses override only specific steps?
questions.explanation: Template Method fixes the overall sequence of steps in a base class method, while individual steps are left as abstract or overridable methods for subclasses to customize.

questions.prompt: Which pattern lets an object appear to change its class by altering its behavior when its internal state changes?
questions.explanation: State encapsulates state-specific behavior into separate state objects; the context delegates to its current state object, so swapping that object changes the context's apparent behavior.

items.title: Singleton implementation approaches
items.context: A naive Singleton with lazy, unsynchronized instantiation isn't thread-safe. Common thread-safe approaches include an eagerly-initialized static field, double-checked locking, the initialization-on-demand holder idiom, or (often recommended in Java) a single-element enum.

questions.prompt: Which approach to implementing a Java Singleton is often recommended for being both lazy and inherently thread-safe with no explicit synchronization?
choices: A plain static field initialized eagerly at class load
A public field with no access control
questions.explanation: A single-element enum gets thread-safe, lazy-enough instantiation handled by the JVM's class-loading guarantees, and even protects against reflection and serialization creating extra instances — a common recommendation for Java specifically.

items.title: Factory Method vs Abstract Factory
items.context: Factory Method defines a single method (often overridden by subclasses) for creating one kind of product. Abstract Factory defines an interface for creating families of related products, without specifying their concrete classes.

questions.prompt: What best distinguishes Abstract Factory from Factory Method?
choices: Abstract Factory creates families of related objects through one interface; Factory Method creates a single kind of object via an overridable method
Abstract Factory is only used for database connections
They are exactly the same pattern
Factory Method can only create Strings
questions.explanation: Factory Method centers on one overridable creation method for one product type; Abstract Factory groups several related creation methods behind one interface, so a client can get a whole consistent family of related objects (e.g. matching UI widgets for a theme) at once.

items.title: Memento pattern
items.context: Memento captures and externalizes an object's internal state into a separate object, so that state can be restored later — without exposing the originating object's internal implementation details to whoever is doing the saving. It's the classic basis for undo/redo functionality.

questions.prompt: What does the Memento pattern let you do?
choices: Add new operations to a class hierarchy without modifying it
Capture and externalize an object's internal state so it can be restored later, without breaking encapsulation
Notify multiple objects of a state change
questions.explanation: Memento snapshots an object's state into a separate, opaque object that the originator can later use to restore itself — enabling undo/rollback functionality without exposing the originator's internals to whatever is storing the snapshot.

items.title: Visitor pattern
items.context: Visitor lets you add new operations to a group of related classes without modifying those classes — each element class implements an accept(Visitor) method that calls back the appropriate visit method on the visitor, based on the element's concrete type.

questions.prompt: What problem does the Visitor pattern solve?
choices: It converts a tree structure into a flat list
It lets you add new operations across a class hierarchy without modifying the classes in that hierarchy
It removes the need for interfaces entirely
It manages object creation for a family of related classes
questions.explanation: Visitor separates an algorithm from the object structure it operates on: new behavior is added by writing a new Visitor implementation, leaving the existing element classes untouched.

questions.prompt: What must each element class implement for the Visitor pattern to work correctly?
choices: An accept(Visitor) method that calls back the correct visit method on the visitor for that element's concrete type
questions.explanation: Each element's accept(visitor) method calls visitor.visit(this) — because 'this' has the element's real compile-time type at that call site, the correct overloaded visit method for that specific element type gets invoked (a technique called double dispatch).

items.title: Dependency Inversion vs Dependency Injection
items.context: Dependency Inversion is a SOLID design principle: high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations. Dependency Injection is one common technique for achieving that principle in practice — supplying an object's dependencies from outside rather than having it construct them itself.

questions.prompt: What's the relationship between the Dependency Inversion Principle and Dependency Injection?
choices: Dependency Injection is a SOLID principle; Dependency Inversion is a coding technique
They are unrelated concepts that happen to share a name
They are exactly the same thing, just different names
Dependency Inversion is the design principle (depend on abstractions); Dependency Injection is a common technique used to achieve it
questions.explanation: Dependency Inversion says high-level code shouldn't depend directly on low-level implementation details, but on abstractions instead; Dependency Injection is the practical mechanism (a framework, or manual wiring) that supplies those abstractions' concrete implementations from outside, achieving the principle.

items.title: Null Object pattern
items.context: Instead of returning null and forcing every caller to null-check, the Null Object pattern returns a special object implementing the same interface but with 'do nothing' (or safely neutral) behavior — eliminating scattered null checks throughout client code.

questions.prompt: What does the Null Object pattern replace null references with?
choices: A real object implementing the same interface, with harmless/no-op behavior, so callers don't need explicit null checks
questions.explanation: A Null Object satisfies the same interface as a real implementation but does nothing (or returns safe defaults), so client code can call methods on it uniformly without special-casing a null check first.

items.title: Repository & DAO patterns
items.context: The DAO (Data Access Object) pattern encapsulates all access to a specific data source behind an interface, hiding persistence details from business logic. The Repository pattern is a closely related, slightly higher-level idea: presenting a collection-like interface (add, remove, find) over the underlying data store — which is exactly the abstraction Spring Data repositories implement.

questions.prompt: What do both the DAO and Repository patterns aim to hide from the rest of the application?
choices: The details of how data is actually accessed and persisted
The network protocol used by the application
questions.explanation: Both patterns put a boundary between business logic and persistence mechanics — code that needs data works against a clean interface (find, save, delete) without knowing or caring whether it's backed by SQL, a file, or an in-memory store.

items.title: MVC as an architectural pattern
items.context: Model-View-Controller separates an application into three responsibilities: the Model holds data and business logic, the View renders it, and the Controller handles input and coordinates between the two — reducing coupling between how data is represented and how it's displayed.

questions.prompt: What are the three responsibilities MVC separates an application into?
questions.explanation: MVC splits data/business logic (Model), presentation (View), and input handling/coordination (Controller) into distinct responsibilities, reducing coupling between how data is stored and how it's shown to a user.

items.title: The 'God Object' anti-pattern
items.context: A God Object is a class that has taken on far too many responsibilities — it knows about and controls large portions of the system, making it a magnet for changes, hard to test in isolation, and a violation of the single-responsibility principle.

questions.prompt: What characterizes the "God Object" anti-pattern?
choices: A single class that has accumulated far too many responsibilities, becoming difficult to maintain, test, and extend
A class with no methods at all
A class implementing the Singleton pattern
questions.explanation: A God Object violates single-responsibility by doing (or knowing about) too much at once — it tends to grow uncontrollably, becomes a bottleneck for changes, and is difficult to unit test in isolation because it's entangled with so much else.

items.title: Bridge pattern
items.context: Bridge decouples an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently — for example, separating 'shape' (circle, square) from 'renderer' (vector, raster) so you can mix and match either dimension without an explosion of subclasses for every combination.

questions.prompt: What problem does the Bridge pattern address?
choices: An explosion of subclasses when a class needs to vary along two independent dimensions, by splitting abstraction from implementation
Notifying many objects of one event
Restricting a class to one instance
questions.explanation: Without Bridge, having N shapes × M renderers naively leads to N×M subclasses; Bridge instead lets the abstraction (shape) hold a reference to an implementation (renderer) interface, so either side can vary and be combined independently.

items.title: Flyweight pattern
items.context: Flyweight minimizes memory usage by sharing as much data as possible between many similar objects — separating intrinsic (shared, immutable) state from extrinsic (context-specific) state that's passed in rather than stored per-instance.

questions.prompt: What is the main goal of the Flyweight pattern?
choices: Reduce memory usage by sharing common (intrinsic) state across many similar objects instead of duplicating it per instance
questions.explanation: Flyweight factors out the state that's identical across many objects (intrinsic state) so it can be shared by reference, while state unique to each usage (extrinsic state) is supplied externally — useful when you'd otherwise need huge numbers of nearly-identical objects, like glyphs in a text editor.

items.title: Iterator pattern
items.context: Iterator provides a uniform way to access a collection's elements sequentially without exposing how that collection is actually implemented internally — exactly what java.util.Iterator abstracts over ArrayList, HashSet, and every other collection type.

questions.prompt: What problem does the Iterator pattern solve?
choices: It restricts a collection to a single element
It lets you traverse a collection's elements sequentially without exposing its internal representation
questions.explanation: Iterator gives every collection a common traversal interface (hasNext()/next()) regardless of whether it's backed by an array, a linked list, or a tree — client code doesn't need to know or care about that internal structure.

items.title: Builder pattern vs telescoping constructors
items.context: The 'telescoping constructor' anti-pattern is a class with many overloaded constructors covering different combinations of optional parameters — it quickly becomes unreadable and error-prone (easy to mix up which positional argument means what). Builder solves this by letting you set only the parameters you care about, by name, before building the final object.

questions.prompt: What specific problem does the Builder pattern solve that a class with many overloaded constructors runs into?
choices: It avoids the 'telescoping constructor' problem — many overloaded constructors for different combinations of optional parameters, which becomes unreadable and error-prone
Builder eliminates the need for any constructor at all
It's only useful for creating a single instance of a class
Builder makes object creation slower on purpose
questions.explanation: Telescoping constructors force callers to remember positional argument order across many overloads; Builder instead lets you call named setter-style methods for only the parameters you actually want to specify, in any order, before finally constructing the object.

items.title: Strategy vs State: similar structure, different intent
items.context: Strategy and State look structurally almost identical (both delegate to a swappable object implementing a common interface), but differ in intent: with Strategy, the client explicitly chooses which algorithm to plug in. With State, the context itself manages its current state object internally, transitioning between states as part of its own lifecycle — the client doesn't pick it.

questions.prompt: Structurally, Strategy and State look very similar. What differentiates them?
choices: They are completely unrelated patterns with no similarity
State is only used for GUI applications
Strategy can only have two possible implementations
Strategy's algorithm is chosen explicitly by the client; State's current state is managed internally by the context itself as part of its lifecycle
questions.explanation: Both patterns delegate behavior to an interchangeable object, but who's in charge of the swap differs: a client picks a Strategy to use for a specific purpose; a context manages its own State transitions internally, often in response to its own events.

items.title: Decorator vs subclassing
items.context: If you need to mix and match several optional behaviors, subclassing for every combination leads to a combinatorial explosion of classes. Decorator instead wraps an object with any number of decorator objects at runtime, composing behaviors dynamically instead of baking every combination into the class hierarchy.

questions.prompt: Why does Decorator often scale better than deep subclassing when you need to combine several optional behaviors?
choices: Subclassing is always faster at runtime
Subclassing needs a new class for every combination of behaviors, while Decorator composes behaviors dynamically at runtime by wrapping objects
Decorator only works with final classes
questions.explanation: With N independent optional behaviors, subclassing for every combination can require up to 2^N classes; Decorator instead lets you wrap an object with whichever combination of decorators you need at runtime, without a matching explosion of statically-defined classes.

items.title: Facade vs Adapter
items.context: Facade's job is to simplify: it presents one easy, unified entry point to a complex subsystem you're not trying to make compatible with anything else. Adapter's job is compatibility: it translates one specific interface into a different one that a client already expects, regardless of complexity.

questions.prompt: What's the core difference in intent between Facade and Adapter?
choices: Adapter can only wrap one class, Facade can wrap many
Facade simplifies access to a complex subsystem; Adapter specifically translates one interface into a different one a client expects
They are exactly the same pattern with different names
Facade is a creational pattern, Adapter is a structural pattern with no other differences
questions.explanation: Facade is about simplification — hiding a subsystem's complexity behind an easy interface. Adapter is about compatibility — converting between two interfaces that don't otherwise match, whether or not the wrapped thing is complex.

items.title: Design patterns in the JDK
items.context: Well-known GoF patterns show up throughout the JDK itself: java.util.Iterator implements Iterator, java.io's BufferedInputStream/InputStreamReader wrapping another stream is Decorator, and Comparator instances passed into Collections.sort() are a form of Strategy.

questions.prompt: Which design pattern does wrapping a FileInputStream in a BufferedInputStream demonstrate?
choices: Decorator — BufferedInputStream adds buffering behavior on top of another InputStream, implementing the same base interface
questions.explanation: BufferedInputStream implements the same InputStream interface as the stream it wraps, and layers new behavior (buffering) on top of it — the textbook shape of the Decorator pattern, used pervasively throughout java.io.

items.title: Mediator pattern
items.context: Mediator centralizes communication between a group of objects into one mediator object, so those objects reference only the mediator instead of each other directly — turning many-to-many coupling into simpler many-to-one coupling.

questions.prompt: What problem does the Mediator pattern address?
choices: Reducing tangled many-to-many references between objects by routing their communication through one central mediator
Ensuring a class has only one instance
Adding new operations to a class hierarchy
questions.explanation: Without Mediator, a set of interacting objects can end up each holding direct references to many others; Mediator collapses that web into a hub-and-spoke shape, where each object only needs to know about the mediator.

items.title: Singleton and testability criticism
items.context: A common criticism of overusing Singleton: it introduces hidden global state and an implicit dependency that's hard to substitute in tests — code calling MySingleton.getInstance() directly can't easily be given a test double the way an injected dependency could.

questions.prompt: What is a common criticism of overusing the Singleton pattern in application code?
choices: It introduces hidden global state and implicit dependencies that are hard to substitute with test doubles
It prevents a class from ever having any methods
Singletons always use too much memory
Singleton can only be implemented in Java
questions.explanation: Because code reaches out and grabs MySingleton.getInstance() directly rather than having the dependency handed to it, that dependency is effectively hidden and global — much harder to swap out for a fake/mock in a unit test than an explicitly injected collaborator.

items.title: Object Pool pattern
items.context: Object Pool reuses a managed set of expensive-to-create objects (database connections, threads) instead of constructing and destroying them repeatedly — directly related to why connection pools and thread pools exist as concrete applications of this idea.

questions.prompt: What is the core idea behind the Object Pool pattern?
choices: Ensuring only one object of a type ever exists
Maintaining a reusable set of expensive-to-create objects, handing them out and reclaiming them instead of constructing/destroying repeatedly
Hiding an object's implementation behind an interface
Creating a brand-new object for every single request
questions.explanation: Object Pool amortizes the cost of expensive object creation (like a database connection) by keeping a managed set of them ready to reuse — exactly the idea behind connection pools and thread pools, both concrete real-world applications of this pattern.

items.title: Composition over inheritance
items.context: "Favor composition over inheritance" is a broad design principle behind many GoF patterns (Strategy, Decorator, Bridge) — building behavior by composing smaller objects together, rather than growing a deep, rigid inheritance hierarchy that's hard to change later.

questions.prompt: Which patterns are commonly cited as concrete examples of favoring composition over inheritance?
choices: None — all GoF patterns rely on inheritance
Strategy and Decorator, which vary behavior by composing in different objects rather than by subclassing
questions.explanation: Strategy and Decorator both achieve flexible, varying behavior by holding a reference to another object (composition) rather than by creating ever-deeper or ever-wider subclass hierarchies — a concrete illustration of why composition is often more flexible than inheritance for varying behavior.

items.title: Reflection breaking a classic Singleton

questions.prompt: What does this print?
choices: false — reflection can call the private constructor directly, breaking the singleton guarantee
true — reflection can't bypass a private constructor
Throws IllegalAccessException, since setAccessible(true) is blocked
questions.explanation: setAccessible(true) lets reflection invoke even a private constructor, creating a second, independent instance — false. An enum-based singleton is immune to this specific attack because the JVM guarantees only one instance per enum constant is ever created, even via reflection.

items.title: Builder leaking a shared mutable field

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: build() hands team1 the exact same mutable List instance the builder keeps holding onto — it never makes a defensive copy. So calling builder.addMember("Bo") after team1 was already built still mutates that shared list, and team1.members shows the change too: [Ann, Bo]. This is a real Builder pitfall — build() should typically return new ArrayList<>(members) (or an unmodifiable view) so a builder can safely be reused or kept around after producing an object.

items.title: Removing an observer during notification

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
choices: Prints A, B only — C never runs
Prints A, B, C with no issues
questions.explanation: Observer B removes an element from the very list being iterated by a for-each loop. Just like any other collection, mutating an ArrayList mid-iteration invalidates the iterator and throws ConcurrentModificationException on the next hasNext()/next() call — a very common real bug in hand-rolled Observer implementations that don't copy the listener list before notifying.

items.title: Shallow clone() sharing a mutable field

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Object.clone() performs a shallow copy: it copies each field's value, but for a reference field like `members`, that means copying the reference itself, not the List it points to. original and copy end up sharing the exact same ArrayList, so mutating copy.members also affects original.members — a classic Prototype-pattern pitfall. A correct clone() would also clone the members list itself (a deep-enough copy).

items.title: Calling `new` on a private constructor

questions.prompt: What happens when this code is compiled?
choices: Compile error: Money() has private access
Compile error: Money is final and can't be instantiated
questions.explanation: The constructor is private, so `new Money(500)` from outside the class is a compile-time error, not a runtime one — the compiler enforces access modifiers statically. Callers are meant to use the public static factory Money.ofCents(...) instead, which is the whole point of this pattern (naming the construction, hiding the implementation, enabling caching/validation).

items.title: Bill Pugh / holder-class Singleton

questions.prompt: Why is this Singleton thread-safe without any explicit synchronized keyword?
choices: The JVM guarantees a nested class is only loaded (and its static fields initialized) the first time it's referenced, and class initialization is inherently thread-safe
getInstance() is implicitly synchronized by the compiler
It isn't actually thread-safe — this is a bug
Holder must be declared volatile for this to work
questions.explanation: This is the "initialization-on-demand holder" idiom. InstanceHolder isn't loaded until getInstance() first references it, and the JLS guarantees the class-loading/initialization process is atomic and thread-safe — the JVM itself handles the locking, once, at class-init time. It gets you lazy initialization and thread safety without any synchronized block or volatile field.

items.title: Iterator not enforcing its next()/hasNext() contract

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
choices: Prints 0, 1, 2 then loops printing increasing numbers forever
questions.explanation: This custom Iterator's next() never checks bounds or throws NoSuchElementException when exhausted — it just keeps incrementing current and returning it, forever. The `while (true)` loop here never calls hasNext(), so nothing stops it. A correct Iterator must throw NoSuchElementException from next() once hasNext() would return false, per the Iterator contract.

items.title: Applying the same Decorator twice

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Each MilkDecorator layer independently adds its own 0.5 on top of whatever it wraps, and nothing stops you from wrapping the same decorator twice. Wrapping SimpleCoffee (2.0) in MilkDecorator twice adds 0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0, giving 3.0 — functionally "double milk", which may or may not be the caller's intent. This is a real risk with decorator chains: nothing at compile time prevents applying the same decorator more times than intended.

items.title: Serialization breaking a Singleton

questions.prompt: What does this print, and why?
choices: false — deserialization invokes no constructor, and instead builds a brand-new instance directly from the byte stream, bypassing the singleton
true — deserialization always returns the same JVM instance for a singleton
questions.explanation: Java deserialization reconstructs an object by reading the stream and populating fields directly — it does not call any constructor or go through getInstance(). So `restored` is a second, independent Config object, breaking the singleton guarantee. The standard fix is adding `private Object readResolve() { return INSTANCE; }`, which deserialization calls (if present) to substitute in the real singleton instead of the freshly built one.

items.title: equals()/hashCode() contract violation in a cache

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: HashMap first narrows its search using hashCode(), then confirms with equals() only among keys sharing that bucket. Here equals() was overridden to compare x/y, but hashCode() was left as Object's default (based on identity) — so `a` and `lookup` are equals()-equal but almost certainly have different hashCodes, land in different buckets, and containsKey() reports false. This is exactly why the equals()/hashCode() contract requires overriding both together, and it silently breaks any HashMap-based cache (like a Flyweight pool) built on such a key.
